entry.title: StepBench: Diagnosing Where AI Agents Go Wrong

link.title: StepBench: Diagnosing Where AI Agents Go Wrong

entry.content:
TL;DR. StepBench turns 6,885 real-world procedures into five diagnostic tasks: last-step selection, missing-step recovery, incorrect-step detection, reordering and next-step generation. It also includes full-plan generation and uses StepEval to identify critical failures in generated plans. Even when every correct step is provided, the best model restores the exact order for only 63.0% of procedures, and scores on the lightweight diagnostic tasks track whether a model’s full plans are valid (Spearman 0.85 to 0.96). The paper, code, dataset, and judge are publicly available.

Imagine a plan for jump-starting a car that reads perfectly. The cables go on in the right order, the working car is left running, and nine of the ten steps are correct. In the tenth step, however, the last black clamp goes on the dead battery’s negative terminal instead of on bare metal away from the battery, where it could spark near the hydrogen the battery releases. A plan like this could match a reference almost word for word and still fail at the one thing that mattered.

As language-model agents take on longer tasks involving tools and actions, planning becomes increasingly important. For everyday, open-domain tasks, however, we usually cannot run a plan at evaluation to verify its validity. Most evaluations therefore evaluate only the final plan, which hides the source of failure: whether the model omitted a step, added an incorrect one, or put the steps in the wrong order.

We therefore asked how much we could learn about the planning abilities of AI agents without having to execute their plans. To answer this question, we introduce StepBench, which turns 6,885 human-written, step-by-step procedures into a set of diagnostic tasks. We pair it with StepEval, a judge that identifies failures in generated plans that would prevent successful task completion.

In this post, we share how we developed StepBench and our key findings. With every correct step provided, the strongest model we tested still restores the right order for only 63.0% of procedures. Scores on these lightweight diagnostic tasks also correlate with whether a model’s full plans are valid. We close with the limitations and several open problems we would love to see the community take on.

Diagnosing where plans fail

Agentic planning can fail in many distinct ways. A plan may leave out a necessary step, include the wrong one, or put the steps in the wrong order. These are different kinds of mistakes, but a final plan-level metric does not show which one a model is making. Two models can therefore end up with the same score for very different reasons.

Distinguishing these failure modes requires knowing where the plan breaks. In settings where a plan can be checked automatically, we can see exactly where it fails. A robot in a simulator either reaches the goal or knocks something over, a block-stacking puzzle comes with a program that rejects any illegal move, and a script can be run to see which command errors out. That is not true for everyday written procedures like making cake flour or checking a Linux machine’s uptime. StepBench gets around this by starting with a verified human procedure and introducing controlled errors, which gives us a known answer without executing the procedure itself.

How we built StepBench

We crawled how-to tasks and kept the articles that describe a genuine procedural task. The result is 6,885 procedures and 30,975 reference steps across 81 categories, averaging 4.5 steps each. From each procedure, we derive five diagnostic tasks. A sixth, full-plan generation, is evaluated alongside them so we can ask whether the diagnostics predict end-to-end quality. Every task draws on the same pool of procedures, so a model’s scores are directly comparable across tasks.

StepEval: Judging Plans that Look Different

T1 to T4 tasks have known answers, but the generated plans do not: a valid plan can word, group, or even order its steps differently from the reference, so text overlap is a poor judge. In our results, Qwen3 4B scores 18.7 ROUGE-L on full plans, the second highest of all configurations, yet only 11.2% of its plans are valid.

StepEval instead asks whether a plan contains a critical failure, an error severe enough to prevent the goal, following the formulation of How2Everything. Harmless variation is accepted. Asked to make cake flour from all-purpose flour, one model repeats the sifting steps and never swaps in cornstarch. That is a critical failure, because sifting alone does not change the flour. Asked to check Linux uptime, another model types uptime where the reference has uptime -p. The output format differs, but you still learn the uptime, so the plan counts as valid.

A model’s valid-plan rate (VPR) is the share of its plans with no critical failure. GPT-5 agrees with the majority of three human annotators on 85.5% of 200 plans. To keep large-scale evaluation affordable, we distilled it into an 8B judge trained on 82K GPT-5 annotations. That judge agrees with GPT-5 on 92% of examples and with the human majority on 82.5%.

What we found

We evaluated 12 models in 14 configurations, counting thinking modes and temperature settings. They range from Llama 3.1 8B to GPT-5.6-sol, Gemini 3 Flash and Cohere’s Command A. The table below gives a compact view of the results, and four findings stand out.

Model Last step (T1) Missing step (T2) Incorrect step (T3) Reordering (T4) Next-step VPR (T5) Full-plan VPR
GPT-5.6-sol 75.7 73.6 66.5 63.0 79.7 92.1
Gemini 3 Flash (thinking, T=0) 78.8 78.2 71.1 58.7 77.0 84.5
Command A Reasoning 67.9 43.9 60.5 51.8 70.0 82.0
Command A 65.5 59.1 61.2 44.3 70.7 67.4
Qwen3 32B (thinking) 65.4 43.6 58.4 49.6 73.3 75.7
Qwen3 14B 53.9 24.9 56.9 45.3 71.5 66.2
Llama 3.1 8B 21.6 26.3 48.0 16.0 50.4 53.6
Qwen3 4B 25.4 28.2 49.7 38.0 64.1 11.2

Selected results for eight of the 14 configurations. T1 to T4 are exact-match accuracy (%), and the two VPR columns are the StepEval valid-plan rate (%). The best score in each column across all 14 configurations is in bold, and random guessing scores 25% on T1 and T2. Full results are in the paper.

Reordering is hard, even when every step is provided. The best configuration, GPT-5.6-sol, restores the exact order for 63.0% of procedures. For that model, accuracy falls from 86.8% at two steps to 33.1% at nine or more. It often lands close to the reference order, but one misplaced step fails an exact match. Exact match is a strict test, since some steps can be swapped without harm.

In the centre panel, exact-order accuracy falls for every model as procedures grow. The right panel shows a gentler decline under edit distance, so models often land near the right order. Incorrect-step detection, on the left, does not follow the same pattern.

Similar plan scores can hide different skills. Command A and Qwen3 14B reach almost the same full-plan VPR (67.4% and 66.2%). Command A recovers a missing step 59.1% of the time, against 24.9% for Qwen3 14B. In a second pair, Qwen3 4B and its Instruct-2507 variant detect incorrect steps equally well (49.7% and 49.9%), yet their full-plan VPR is 11.2% and 57.3%.

Reasoning helps unevenly. Command A Reasoning beats Command A on full-plan VPR (82.0% against 67.4%) and on reordering (51.8% against 44.3%). Its missing-step recovery, though, falls from 59.1% to 43.9%. These are different model variants, so the comparison does not isolate the effect of reasoning.

Diagnostic scores correlate with plan validity. Across the 14 configurations, every diagnostic rises with full-plan VPR. The Spearman correlations are 0.96 for reordering, 0.95 for last-step selection, 0.93 for incorrect-step detection, 0.89 for next-step VPR and 0.85 for missing-step recovery. T1 to T4 need no judge and no generation, making them a lightweight way to obtain an early read on overall planning ability. The pattern holds across models; it does not promise that a model succeeds on every plan it could order correctly.

Two configurations break the pattern. Qwen3 4B orders steps about as well as its peers but produces valid plans only 11.2% of the time, while Llama 3.1 8B orders worst (16.0%) yet reaches 53.6% valid plans. Rank correlation tolerates a few outliers like these, which is one reason to read the profile rather than a single number.

Could memorisation explain the results?

The source articles are public, so some models may have seen these procedures during training. To probe thi, we built StepBench-Val: 214 procedures and 1,034 steps from 94 articles published in 2026, spanning 27 of the main categories.

After matching category mix and procedure length, accuracy on T1 to T3 moves by 1.4 points or less on average. Reordering drops 8.3 points, and next-step VPR drops 7.5. Full-plan VPR falls 16.2 points, a gap we do not fully explain. Model rankings stay largely intact, with rank correlations between 0.77 and 0.99 across the diagnostics.

StepBench-Val is a smaller set built from newer articles, so we treat it as a robustness check rather than a full contamination test. The main takeaway is that model rankings remain stable on fresh data. We expect absolute scores, especially for reordering and full plans, to be somewhat sensitive to what models saw in training.

Limitations and what comes next

StepBench covers English-language procedures from a single public source, mostly everyday tasks, and the procedures are short (4.5 steps on average). StepEval depends on the quality of its reference and on judgements about what counts as acceptable variation, and its 82.5% agreement with the human majority leaves room for error. Exact-match ordering penalises plans whose steps could be swapped harmlessly. Compute and API budgets also limited how many models and configurations we could run. These gaps point to problems we would love to see the community explore:

  • Other languages and sources. Do the same diagnostic profiles appear for procedures written in other languages, or drawn from specialised domains?
  • Longer, harder plans. Reordering gets harder as procedures grow. What happens on plans with dozens of steps, branches or tool calls?
  • Interchangeable steps. Annotating which steps can be reordered would turn exact match into a fairer test of ordering.
  • Human baselines. How do people score on T1 to T4, and where do models and people fail differently?

Try it yourself

Everything is open: the corpus, the task files for all five diagnostic tasks and full-plan generation, model outputs, judge annotations and analysis code. The paper provides the prompts, evaluation settings, and fuller analyses behind the results discussed here.

  • Paper: arxiv.org/abs/2610.26679
  • Code: github.com/rahmanidashti/StepBench
  • StepBench: StepBench on Hugging Face
  • StepEval: StepEval on Hugging Face

Each task is its own configuration, with a test split (the main benchmark) and a validation split (StepBench-Val):

from datasets import load_dataset

 reorder = load_dataset(
 	"rahmanidashti/StepBench",
 	"task4_step_reordering",
 	split="test",
 )
 print(reorder[0]["method_title"])

One caution: records hold both task inputs and reference answers. Build prompts from the model-visible fields listed in the dataset card, never from whole records, or the answer leaks into the prompt.

Reproducibility at a glance

Data. 6,885 procedures, 30,975 steps and 81 categories. The main benchmark is the test split, and StepBench-Val (214 procedures from 94 articles published in 2026) is the validation split. Each task is its own Hugging Face configuration. A GPT-4.1 filter selected genuine procedural tasks, and distractors are retrieved from other procedures in the same category.

Models. 12 models in 14 configurations: Qwen3 4B, 8B, 14B and 32B, Qwen3 4B Instruct 2507, Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, Gemma 3 27B, GLM-4 9B, GPT-5.6-sol, Gemini 3 Flash, Command A and Command A Reasoning. Exact model IDs are in the paper.

Decoding. Greedy decoding (T=0) unless a provider requires otherwise, plus one sampled configuration (Gemini 3 Flash at T=1) to check that conclusions do not depend on greedy decoding. Qwen3 32B is run with and without thinking, while Command A Reasoning and Gemini 3 Flash are run in thinking mode only. All models share the same prompts and parsers, and the prompts are listed in the paper appendix.

Scoring. Exact match for T1 to T4, with normalised edit distance also reported for reordering. Outputs that cannot be parsed count as incorrect. Next-step and full-plan outputs are scored by StepEval valid-plan rate (Qwen3 8B fine-tuned on GPT-5 annotations, decoded with T=0, top-p 0.95 and top-k 20), with ROUGE and BERTScore reported as secondary metrics.

Acknowledgements

StepBench is a joint work with Bin Wu, Chaeeun Lee, Fanghua Ye, Sahan Bulathwela, Sujay Kumar Jauhar, Marzieh Fadaee, Nick Craswell and Emine Yilmaz. This research is supported in part by the Cohere Labs Catalyst Grant Program, by the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EP/S021566/1) and the EPSRC Fellowship “Task Based Information Retrieval” (EP/P024289/1), and by NVIDIA DGX Spark compute provided for the grant “Agentic Evaluation: Efficient and Reliable Evaluation for Agentic AI Systems”.

Disclosure. Command A and Command A Reasoning, two of the models we evaluate, are Cohere models, and Marzieh Fadaee, one of our co-authors, is at Cohere Labs. All models were run with identical prompts, parsers and judges, and funding from the Cohere Labs Catalyst Grant Program does not imply endorsement of the results.
entry.summary: StepBench tests where AI agents' plans break by asking models to recover, repair and reorder the steps of 6,885 real-world procedures, instead of grading only the final plan.

entry.title: Does a Model Hold the Stereotype Even When It Doesn’t Say It? Probing Social Bias with the Jacobian Lens

link.title: Does a Model Hold the Stereotype Even When It Doesn’t Say It? Probing Social Bias with the Jacobian Lens

entry.content:
TL;DR

  • Yes, sometimes. In Qwen3.5-4B, stereotype-congruent tokens surface in the Jacobian-lens workspace even when the output never states them, and even when the context has already settled the answer.
  • Gender is the clearest case. The lens’s gendered preference for each occupation tracks US labor statistics (Spearman ρ rises from +0.332 at layer 20 to +0.681 at layer 29), while a permuted-Jacobian null stays flat.
  • Beyond gender, the evidence is fragile. On the balanced BBQ benchmark we found no significant aggregate signal. Baseline group preferences explain 63–98% of the variance, and the choice of descriptor word (“weak” vs. “submissive”) can move the readout more than the choice of group.
  • There is no single “bias layer.” Correlations peak around layers 23–25, layer 27 makes both answers accessible at once, and steering works best at layers 29–30.
  • The lens is a causal handle, but a blunt one. Swapping lens directions changes answers, yet most of the effect comes from ablating the answer the model was already giving. At large intervention strengths (α ≥ 3) the output falls apart.
  • The method lesson: a lens readout must be treated as evidence, rather than proof. We recommend triangulating across lenses, controls and datasets.

At a glance

Research question Short answer Section
RQ1. Do stereotype-congruent tokens surface in the lens? Yes, most clearly for gender and occupations. Aggregate significance on balanced datasets is contingent on measurement choices. RQ1
RQ2. Where in the network does the signal show up? Mostly late-intermediate layers (≈23–30), but the band depends on axis, metric and prompt format. RQ2
RQ3. How do context, wording, format and pressure reshape it? A lot. Descriptor wording, prompt format and pressure often matter more than group identity. RQ3
RQ4. Does the signal causally drive the answer? Partly. Lens directions are a handle on the committed answer, but swaps add little beyond ablation. RQ4

Why look inside the model?

Most bias benchmarks, such as BBQ , judge a model only by its final answer. That tells us what the model says, not what it considered along the way. A model can give an acceptable answer while still holding a stereotyped idea internally, and a final-answer score will never show it.

This post summarizes a multi-week Cohere Labs Community project that tries to look at that process. We use the Jacobian lens (J-lens) to ask whether stereotype-related content can be detected inside a model, where it appears, how it changes with context, and whether it actually drives the answer. All code and materials are in the group repository.

Background - reading the workspace with the J-lens

In July 2026, Anthropic’s interpretability team published Verbalizable Representations Form a Global Workspace in Language Models . The paper borrows an idea from cognitive science, Global Workspace Theory: many processes run in parallel and stay hidden, but a small set of information is shared widely and is available for reporting. The authors ask whether language models have something that plays a similar functional role. They make no claim that models have experiences. The question is strictly about computation.

To explore this, they introduce the J-lens and the related J-space, and test the workspace-like properties of that space with causal interventions, not only correlations. The tool is released as the open-source jacobian-lens library. We use it with a pre-fitted lens on Qwen3.5-4B.

How the lens works. A model produces its answer one token at a time, but most of the computation happens in the residual stream of the hidden layers, where nothing is printed. The classic logit lens reads this stream by applying the unembedding matrix directly at an intermediate layer, which gets unreliable in early layers because the stream does not use the same coordinates at every layer.

The J-lens instead describes an activation through its first-order causal effect on the model’s outputs. Let h_{\ell,t} be the residual stream at layer \ell and position t. A small change to it shifts the final-layer stream at all later positions t' \ge t, and to first order that effect is a Jacobian. A Jacobian from one prompt mixes the model’s general disposition to say a concept with how that concept is used in that context, so the paper averages over source positions, later positions and a corpus of one thousand pretraining-like prompts:

J_\ell = \mathbb{E}_{t,\, t' \ge t,\, \text{prompt}} \left[ \frac{\partial h_{\text{final},t'}}{\partial h_{\ell,t}} \right], \qquad \mathrm{lens}(h_\ell) = \mathrm{softmax}\big(W_U \, \mathrm{norm}(J_\ell h_\ell)\big)

The result is a score for every vocabulary token: the words the activation is, on average across contexts, disposed to make the model say. The logit lens is the special case J_\ell = I.

This lets us see concepts that never appear in the input or the output. In the paper’s example, the prompt “The number of legs on the animal that spins webs is” surfaces spider in intermediate layers, though the word is in neither the prompt nor the answer. This means we can look for the stereotype the model considered but did not say.

Caveat. The authors describe the J-lens as an imperfect, approximate tool, and its readouts are noisy in roughly the first third of the model. We take this into consideration throughout the experiment.

Setup

Models and lenses. Most experiments use Qwen3.5-4B with the released qwen-n1000 J-lens. A few smaller checks use Qwen3.5-0.8B and we say so where they appear. We also built a second lens, the template lens, to fix a coverage gap. The J-lens is undefined whenever the two answers in a BBQ item share a first token (for example, “grandfather” and “grandson” both start with “grand”), which drops its usable coverage to as low as 19 of 40 quads in some categories. The template lens is made of 833 phrase-level vectors fit from passages generated by Qwen-3.6-27B, and it scores all 40 quads by comparing answers at the first word where they actually differ.

Both lenses pass a basic validity check: on disambiguated items their readouts lean toward whichever answer the text supports, in all 11 BBQ categories, while multiple-choice accuracy on those items ranges from 0.79 to 0.96. They differ in reliability. The J-lens readout correlates with what the model actually generates far more consistently (0.57 to 0.89 across categories) than the template lens does (−0.02 to 0.61). The two are complementary, not interchangeable.

Data. BBQ (age, disability status, nationality, physical appearance, religion, sexual orientation, SES, gender identity and more), Winogender with US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) occupational gender data, CrowS-Pairs-style prompts, hand-built South Asian workplace-leadership cloze prompts, and multilingual sets (Urdu, Chinese C-BBQ, and Indic-Bias with a custom Sarvam-1 lens). WikiText passages serve only as a control corpus for frequency matching and fluency checks.

Reading the numbers. Several layer bands were chosen after looking at results, and some tests are small. We flag these as exploratory throughout. Treat them as hypotheses for preregistered follow-up.

RQ1 - Do stereotype-congruent tokens surface?

We first asked whether stereotype-congruent concepts become readable in intermediate and late representations even when the final output does not state them.

Gender is where the signal is clearest

Take a BBQ item that asks whether a man or a woman is the secretary, where the context gives no way to decide. Across layers 14–31, the answer-letter token for the woman appeared six times in the lens readout, and the man’s once. The lean persists when the context settles the question. In an item stating that the boy is bad at math, the letter for “girl” still showed up three times in the workspace, against five for the correct answer. The model answers correctly, yet the stereotype-congruent option stays readable internally.

Hand-picked examples can mislead, so we aggregated. Our most robust finding compares the lens’s gendered preference for each occupation with BLS data. Spearman’s ρ rises from +0.332 at layer 20 to +0.681 at layer 29 (p < 0.001), tracking the point where the pronoun becomes the top-ranked token (around layer 28). To check that this reflects learned structure and not an artifact of projecting through any matrix of that size, we built a permuted-Jacobian null matched in norm and spectrum. Its correlation stays flat and non-significant (+0.157 down to +0.022, all p > 0.22). The J-lens also surfaces the association about six layers earlier than the standard logit lens, which reads nothing at layers 20–23.

One result surprised us. Final-layer behavior correlates with occupational statistics more strongly (ρ = +0.789) than the intermediate workspace does (ρ = +0.560). This cuts against the common assumption that intermediate layers hide a stronger bias than the model expresses. Here, the internal signal looks like an earlier, noisier, attenuated version of the bias in behavior.

A Winogender follow-up points the same way, though less firmly. Scoring full sentences (which keeps the suffix that identifies the pronoun’s antecedent) over 120 matched pairs, the mean female-minus-male log-likelihood was −1.418 nats for occupation antecedents and −1.103 for participant antecedents. The paired difference of −0.314 nats (95% CI [−0.679, +0.036], Wilcoxon p = 0.069) leans male for occupations, but the interval includes zero, so it is suggestive, not conclusive.

Beyond gender: intersectional, religious and age stereotypes

Intersectionality. Adding racial and ethnic descriptors to the “bad at math” item left stereotype-congruent tokens ahead in most variants, even though the context says the boy struggles. But placing “Latino” or “Indian” before “girl” flipped the balance toward counter-stereotype tokens, and “boy” surfaced correctly at layer 31. In the secretary item the descriptors added variation, and the effect vanished once the answer options were removed from the prompt.

In a second analysis, eight English workplace-leadership cloze prompts compared a South Asian woman with a South Asian man (248 prompt-layer observations). The lens ranked the counter-stereotype descriptor above the stereotype one for both (mean logit gap −1.32; −1.33 for the woman, −1.31 for the man). The woman-minus-man difference sits near zero through layer 9, dips slightly in layers 10–19, and turns positive in layers 25–30 (mean +0.42, peaking at +0.67 at layer 29), where the lens agrees most with the model’s output. In short, a gendered asymmetry can survive in intersectional settings, concentrated in late layers, but an ethnic descriptor can also erase or reverse it. Single-axis readings should not be assumed to carry over.

Religion was the strongest candidate outside gender. A raw lens delta mixes a baseline preference for one group’s term regardless of the question (a group prior) with a polarity-dependent preference that actually tracks the stereotype (a bias term). Decomposing ambiguous BBQ items this way, the group prior explains 63–98% of between-item variance across categories, with gender identity highest (0.98 for the J-lens). Religion has the lowest group-prior share (0.63), and the template lens also tracks the model’s generations well there. That makes it the best candidate for a genuine stereotype signal, but only a candidate: religion’s readout also shifted substantially with question polarity, and some of that may reflect the target’s semantic role, not a stable stereotype.

Age was harder. On 40 BBQ Age items at layer 30, ambiguous items were dominated by hedges such as “unclear” and “neither.” Identity terms appeared in the top 20 for 23 of 40 items (57.5%), but stereotype and counter-stereotype terms usually appeared together. Only the disambiguated/negative cell clearly favored the stereotype (mean rank gap +269, median +110.5), and with ten items per cell and a few outliers that could easily be noise. Steering tells a similar story: a difference-of-means age direction at layer 8 turned a hedged answer into a confident counter-stereotype one on one item, but across 15 items random directions of equal norm matched or beat it at layers 8 and 15. Only at layer 22 did it beat every random control (override rate 0.40 vs. 0.20). A single striking example, without random-direction controls, was weak evidence.

Why the aggregate signal is hard to pin down

We consistently found stereotype-associated tokens in individual prompts, but not always a statistically significant aggregate. In balanced datasets, each group appears equally often in stereotyped and non-stereotyped roles, so effects partly cancel across prompts. A full BBQ 2×2 on Qwen3.5-4B (350 items, 7 categories, all layers) found no aggregate signal at the answer position: the pooled layer-23 median gap on ambiguous items was −64 with 46% positive, and the lens override rate ran opposite to behavior (46.8% disambiguated vs. 21.4% ambiguous). The gaps live in the far tail: the lens puts the stereotype word at median rank around 8,000 of 248k, where the model’s own readout puts it near 111.

Several measurement obstacles make this worse:

  • Hedging. When the options include “not enough information,” models tend to produce output consistent with hedging instead of committing.
  • Token importance. Stereotype-congruent and counter-stereotype tokens both rank low relative to other tokens, including non-semantic ones.
  • Fragmentation. Words split across tokens, and multi-word answers can share a first token, muddying top-token analysis.
  • Word lists overstate direction. In a quantitative pass over free-response readouts, the top-10 tokens were mostly neutral hedges, and only 16–19% leaned stereotype-congruent.

RQ2 - Where in the network does it show up?

There is no single answer, and the layer you find depends on what you measure.

Correlation peaks mid-to-late. In one BBQ and Winogender analysis, balanced gender preference peaked at 0.588 in layers 23–25 (a score where 0.5 means no signal). The BLS correlation rises through layer 29. Pronoun accessibility changes sharply near layer 28, where the pronoun’s rank moves from 233 at layer 0 to 1, and its emergence tracks the occupational correlation profile (rs = +0.821).

Layer 27 exposes both answers. Across seven BBQ datasets, the strongest transition under the answer-text prompt (P2) occurs from layer 26 to 27, where bias and non-bias targets both move toward the top of the vocabulary (cross-dataset mean changes of −1.254 and −1.220). It appears in all seven datasets and under P3 as well.

Dataset Bias target Non-bias target
Age −0.869 −0.801
Physical appearance −1.262 −1.213
Religion −1.396 −1.369
Disability status −0.831 −0.810
Nationality −1.228 −1.227
Sexual orientation −1.684 −1.657
Socioeconomic status −1.505 −1.461

Change in target accessibility from layer 26 to 27 (negative means closer to the top of the vocabulary).

Because both alternatives become accessible together, layer 27 is better read as a task-relevant semantic workspace than as a “stereotype layer.” Bias, where present, is a relative imbalance between jointly accessible targets.

Correlation is not causal leverage. Correlational readouts peak around layers 23–25, but sub-band steering puts the strongest causal leverage later. Intervening only at layers 29–30 reproduced the full eleven-layer steering effect (+2.53 nats), while steering layers 20–25 had little effect (+0.43 to +0.58 nats; 15–20% answer flips). Counterfactual patching, which writes the matched disambiguated residual into an ambiguous prompt, raised evidence-supported answers from under 10% in the earliest layers to about 63% by the low twenties, 71% at layer 27 and 76% at layer 31. The template lens stabilized around layer 23, although patching had already shifted half the prompts by layer 19. So the lens is a delayed correlate of the decision, not a live trace of it.

Early structure can reverse. For South Asian workplace prompts, the English woman-minus-man gap was near zero in layers 0–9 and positive in layers 25–30. Urdu prompts looked different: the woman answer led at layers 0–2 (+2.92 at layer 0), then the preference reversed at layer 3 and stayed negative through layer 30. Early signals can change direction instead of growing into the later English pattern. Age results resist localization altogether: across 40 prompts on Qwen3.5-0.8B, rank gaps varied by item and layer, formatting tokens often outranked both targets, and the largest gap was selected after scanning layers, so we treat them as descriptive only.

Late layers can undo early signals. One multi-band ablation found no output change from layers 0–20, with steerability concentrated in layers 22–30. In the patching curve, the largest single jump (23% to 41%) came at layer 17, a linear-attention layer, in a model that alternates attention types every four layers. Long-range mixing is a possible explanation, but this is preliminary.

Taken together, the evidence supports a late-intermediate workspace for several 4B signals, not one universal localization. The apparent band depends on axis, read position, prompt format and metric. Because several band edges were chosen after inspecting results, treat them as hypotheses, not architectural boundaries.

RQ3 - What changes the signal?

If the signal were a stable property of the model, it should survive reasonable changes to the prompt. It mostly does not.

Wording and framing beat group identity. We scored four English workplace scenarios, each with its own descriptor pair, for a South Asian woman and man (logit gap averaged over 31 layers). The descriptor pair set the sign of the gap for both groups. “Submissive/assertive” and “timid/confident” favored the counter-stereotype word (about −4.2 and −2.9 for the woman, −3.9 and −2.4 for the man), while “indecisive/decisive” and “weak/strong” leaned toward the stereotype word (+0.34 and +1.48 for the woman, +0.32 and +0.76 for the man). The woman-minus-man difference was small and changed direction across scenarios (−0.24, −0.55, +0.02, +0.72). Each scenario had only one descriptor pair, so wording and framing are confounded, and separating them would need several pairs per scenario. Three Urdu prompts showed a layer-dependent reversal (woman favored in layers 0–2, man from layer 3), but with n = 3 that is only suggestive.

Pressure moves the commitment layer. In a multi-turn adversarial-pressure sequence on Qwen3.5-4B, the layer where P(she) first exceeds 80% moved earlier, from layer 28 to layer 24. Concretely, P(she) was 84.1% at layer 28 in the neutral prompt, 81.0% at layer 24 under explicit pressure, and reached 97.9% at layer 28. This is a condition-specific trajectory, not a universal layer boundary. The late-layer pattern carried over beyond English (Chinese C-BBQ, Indic languages, Urdu), with language-specific biases in intermediate layers and late-workspace rank gaps on Indic-Bias.

Measurement choices move the signal.

  • Where you read. The signal sits at the answer slot and is neutral at entity positions (0.500 ± 0.002).
  • Prompt format. Going from multiple-choice to free-form drops the signal from 0.588 to 0.527. The answer-text (P2) and concise (P3) prompts made targets most readable, and the multiple-choice prompt (P1) the least. Median target rank was 295.5 for bare prompts, 30.5 for chat-formatted and 9.0 for raw.
  • Answer-choice structure. Dropping the whole (a)/(b)/(c) block reduced the rank-gap magnitude substantially: in 37 of 40 matched pairs the open-ended band average was smaller in absolute value, and its sign matched the multiple-choice sign in all 40. This is a narrow test (one model, Qwen3.5-0.8B; one category, BBQ Age; ten base items; an exploratory L15–L22 band; no generated answers scored), so it shows that option letters inflate readouts, not that bias was reduced.
  • Ambiguity and polarity. Age and Nationality showed the expected ambiguity pattern, SES weakened but persisted, and Disability Status and Sexual Orientation barely moved. Polarity flipped signs in places (Sexual Orientation went from −0.006490 to +0.009104).
  • Evidence. On disambiguated BBQ items, accuracy was 0.843 when the evidence confirmed the stereotype and 0.909 when it contradicted it, with twice as many “unknown” answers in the confirming case.

Across RQ3, the stereotype signal was sensitive to context, wording and format, and far less to group identity alone. Some apparent identity effects may be artifacts of how we measured.

RQ4 - Does the signal drive the answer?

Correlation is not mechanism, so we intervened on lens-derived and contrastive directions: ablation, difference-of-means steering, coordinate swapping between paired tokens, and targeted suppression. We tracked both J-space and output-token effects. Most experiments use Qwen3.5-4B with the qwen-n1000 J-lens and the template lens. The swap study uses BBQ matched quads (12 quads in each of 11 categories, 132 in total; evidence changed the named group in 119 pairs, and 71 prompts were eligible with an unedited group answer), and the gender-axis study uses Winogender (120 occupation-antecedent prompts).

Getting the swap right

For two answer directions \mathbf{V}=[\mathbf{v}_s,\mathbf{v}_t], the coordinates of a residual are \mathbf{c}=\mathbf{V}^{\dagger}\mathbf{h}. A clean pass caches the clean coordinates at each edited layer. On the intervention pass, the two cached coordinates are exchanged by a swap σ, and the residual is updated as:

\mathbf{h} \leftarrow \mathbf{h} + \alpha \mathbf{V}\big(\sigma(\mathbf{c}_{\text{clean}}^{[\ell]}) - \mathbf{c}\big)

At α = 1 this writes the exchanged coordinates into the two-direction subspace and leaves everything orthogonal untouched. The J-lens paper gave limited implementation detail, and our first attempt (a single-pass swap, where each layer reads coordinates from the already-edited residual) worked for point-wise swaps but broke across layer bands. Each layer sees an already-swapped pair and swaps it back, so the sign alternates from layer to layer. At α = 1 the alternation keeps the edit small. Above α = 1 each layer also overshoots, the alternation grows instead of cancelling, and the residual moves 1.5× and 33× its norm at α = 1.5 and 2. Our two-pass version records clean coordinates for every layer in the band first, then applies the edit. It reproduced the original paper’s results, which confirmed our implementation.

What the controls say

We checked that the pipeline responds to a known manipulation (subtracting directly from the stereotype token’s logit shifted the mean logit gap by an equal amount), then added controls: a random-token swap (does any added content work?), a nonce control (does any real-seeming content work?), and a Gaussian-direction swap, which acts as an approximate, leaky ablation that removes the target’s component without adding anything specific. We also used patching as a positive control.

The picture is humbling:

  • Ablation does most of the work. Ablating the direction of the answer the model currently gives changes about half of answers or more, whether or not it is the stereotyped one. Neither the J-lens nor the template lens swap beats the ablation of the given answer’s direction, and adding the other group’s direction on top adds nothing measurable. The model moves to its next-ranked answer, usually the other group, sometimes a hedge (up to about 20% of answers for J-lens ablations and 3% for template ablations). Ablating the answer that is not on top almost never changes anything.
  • But the handle is real. That asymmetry shows an answer’s lens direction is a working handle on the committed answer, not just a readout.
  • Lenses differ. The J-lens swap clears its real-vector controls (random token 11%, unrelated group 17%), though those controls also badly degrade the text. The template lens swap does not clear a random word’s template, plausibly because its edited coordinate is small relative to the residual. J-lens swaps work about as well on multi-token terms as single-token ones, which suggests the first token carries the rest of the phrase.

Where and how hard to intervene

Swaps are strongest late in the network. Single-layer swaps work within the workspace band, especially layers 20–30, while interventions at layers 1–5 leave the final-layer readout unchanged. That means either this band is too early to act directly on the output, or the model recovers the concept downstream. We cannot yet say which.

Dose matters, and damage is easy. On Winogender, a he/she coordinate swap across layers 20–30 shifts the mean log p(she) − log p(he) by +1.78, +2.53, +3.18 and +4.25 nats at α = 0.5, 1, 1.5 and 2, reversing the preference in 85–96% of the 120 prompts, while frequency-matched sham and norm-matched random controls stay near zero. From about α = 2.75 the lens readout starts oscillating between source- and target-token variants, and at α ≥ 3 KL divergence spikes, held-out WikiText loss degrades, and the sham pair spuriously triggers 77.5% flips. Any effect at α ≥ 3 reflects generalized damage, not targeted axis control, so we treat α ≤ 2 as the safe range. Note too that the swap inverts a direction; it is not evidence of demographic parity.

A statistical direction is not enough. A difference-of-means direction learned from 240 paired male/female-pronoun sentences was internally consistent (pair cosine peaking at layers 26–29), yet at α = 1 it shifted preference by only +0.26 nats with 32% flips (KL = 0.058), far below the lens swap (+2.53 nats, ~96% flips). A direction that merely separates examples is a weaker handle than one built to alter output logits.

Late layers hold bias in more than one direction. Late layers appear to store the signal in a multi-dimensional subspace that one direction can reduce but not remove, and edits in middle layers can be undone downstream. In one case, ablating the single token “he” cut P(she) from 44.6% to 17.7%, which points to grammatical entanglement, while subtracting the she-minus-he difference vector moved P(she) to 7.9% and raised P(he) from 1.5% to 48.8%. Strong flips can also push activations off-distribution, so flip rate alone can overstate success.

Considerations

  • Stereotype detection depends on it. Top-ranked-token analysis can miss stereotype-congruent tokens that rank low, single-token readouts break on first-token sharing, and hedging vocabulary can mask group preferences.
  • A template approach captures multi-word group terms that the J-lens misses, while the J-lens tracks generations more reliably. We recommend using complementary lenses for analysis.
  • It’s always recommended to include controls. Random-direction, frequency-matched, permuted-Jacobian and Gaussian controls each overturned or weakened a result that looked convincing without them.
  • Separate group priors from polarity-dependent bias, and we found that most of a raw delta’s variance is prior.

Limitations and open problems

  • Scale and family. Our tests focus on small open models from one family. Do these patterns hold in larger models or other families?
  • Intersectionality deserves more attention. Adding racial and ethnic categories to our gender analysis preserved the gender pattern but also produced variation and reversals. Adding categories such as Indian and South Asian to BBQ’s race/ethnicity subset turned up results worth following.
  • What makes a good dataset? Balanced datasets cancel stereotyped and non-stereotyped roles, which hides signals that may matter more for groups stereotyped more often. Datasets built from real-world tasks where LLMs are actually deployed would give a more grounded, if narrower, answer to whether models are biased, and would be a major contribution.
  • Better lenses. The J++ lens improves early-layer reliability, filters non-semantic tokens, and has been used to reveal concepts a model suppresses, which could make stereotype-congruent and counter-stereotypical tokens easier to access.
  • Confirmatory work. Many of our layer bands and small-sample results are exploratory and need preregistered follow-up.

Conclusion

A model can answer correctly and still hold the stereotype. That is what the J-lens lets us see: in Qwen3.5-4B, stereotype-congruent content surfaces in the workspace even when the output never states it, and even when the context has already settled the question.

The strongest case is gender, where the lens’s occupational preferences track US labor statistics and a permuted null stays flat. Step outside that setting and the signal gets slippery: in balanced datasets like BBQ, stereotyped and counter-stereotyped cases cancel, group priors absorb most of the variance, and a change of descriptor can move the readout more than a change of group. Where the signal lives is equally layered. Correlations peak around layers 23–25, layer 27 lights up both answers at once, and steering is most effective at layers 29–30. Lens directions give us a handle on the committed answer, but a swap adds little beyond ablating the answer the model was already giving, and at α ≥ 3 the output loses coherence.

The lesson is less about any single number than about method. A readout is evidence, not a verdict. Finding bias in a model’s inner workings means triangulating across lenses, controls and datasets, and testing whether the signal actually drives the answer or merely sits beside it.
entry.summary: A community study of whether stereotype-congruent concepts surface in the internal workspace of Qwen3.5, where they appear, what shapes them, and whether they actually drive the model's answers.

entry.title: FeatureGraph: Automating Scientific and Engineering Time-Series Analysis

link.title: FeatureGraph: Automating Scientific and Engineering Time-Series Analysis

entry.content:
The problem we want to solve

Scientific and engineering timeseries data analysis is not standardized, which means researchers carry out a lot of repeated ad hoc coding work and end up with data artifacts that diverge and create multiple sources of truth. FeatureGraph can start to solve the problem by standardizing researcher work and creating a single source of truth for computed and derived analysis.

Here’s a familiar experience for a lot of researchers and data scientists:

Researcher work and ad hoc analysis gets thrown away, forgotten, and carried out again and again. The same people on the same team are writing slightly different code, the same problems are being solved over and over, and boilerplate code gets reused in slightly different forms. Code regularly gets written to be used for one analysis or study and called up again months later, and often the work is saved in a notebook using outdated code on previous versions of the data, broken dependencies, or logic that no longer applies.

Divergent data sources create multiple sources of truth. Teams sometimes try to sidestep the problem of disposable code buried in notebooks by creating reusable centralized code libraries. But disposable code is only part of the issue. The other, far more consequential part is the data artifacts teams create, including not only static files but databases and data services accessible to downstream users. These created artifacts, which all serve as sources of truth, get handed around, diverge from each other, and get recreated with different expectations.

Computations and derivations disagree and are therefore not trusted. A research team within an organization makes its own decisions on computation parameters, and those decisions are often not cross-compared with those of other research groups. When different teams give slightly or even significantly different answers to the same question, there is not always an obvious way to track where the disagreement came from.

The problem is invisible until it isn’t. Timeseries derivations slowly and imperceptibly become less trustworthy the less reproducible they are and the more potential sources of truth exist. A team only becomes aware of the scope of the problem when a study or report expected to take hours to produce ends up taking days or weeks because the “correct” numbers have to be hunted down.

The project

FeatureGraph proposes to build a solution for two aspects of the problem: the repeated construction of derivations from timeseries scientific and engineering data, and how that derived work is accessed. It provides a persistent store both where raw timeseries data is automatically processed and summarized and where the results of previous analysis work are verified, recorded, and immediately available as one source of truth.

Research teams run analyses and derive results the same way every time, using explicit sets of construction assumptions. They query the results of each analysis from one place where its provenance is clearly defined. Provenance, assumptions, and accuracy can be tracked and verified by construction.

By coupling construction and access, assumptions can be changed and a study rerun from the same access point with minimal work. Even studies that genuinely need to be carried out multiple times in slightly different ways are all recorded, stored, and accessed from the same source. An analysis on the same data that needs different smoothing window parameters, sampling intervals, or summary-level filters creates a new defined study, so the difference is visible and recorded.

An additional benefit of using FeatureGraph is the ability to natively automate research tasks with AI agents in constrained workflows, allowing language models to construct and use the same derived studies as human researchers. Ongoing development on this is discussed in later sections.

How it works

FeatureGraph takes a raw timeseries recording or data column and produces an object-level summary. An object is an identifiable event in a timeseries signal described by properties like its height, duration, and shape. The example below illustrates how a timeseries oscillation signal such as human breathing can be split into individual waves, each called an object.

The same object creation logic gets applied to other oscillatory behaviors like pressure changes in an industrial reactor or mechanical pulses from a rotating drill string. Object construction depends only on the shape of the signal and not on outside context, so the process is domain-agnostic and the accuracy of the derived properties can be traced directly back to the construction parameters, such as smoothing window sizes and detected periodicity of the wave.

Non-oscillatory signal behavior patterns are also in use as object construction templates, and objects other than individual waves can be created from oscillatory signals, but that is not discussed in this post.

BIDMC and CapnoBase are two public datasets of respiration recordings that measure breathing using different signals and sampling frequencies. FeatureGraph works in one-second intervals for both datasets, so the same measures can be computed on each.

Because the construction depends only on the shape of the signal and not on outside context, the results can be traced back to the construction parameters. Each summary is stored and can be queried through the data service.

A technical look into FeatureGraph

FeatureGraph has two parts: the compiler and the query layer. The compiler turns timeseries data into explicit objects, and the query layer allows the objects to be delivered in an analysis.

The compiler: P/D/O/M/S

Every object FeatureGraph produces moves through five layers. The first four layers of the compiler are built, fully deterministic, and run completely outside any language model. The fifth layer is being built to work with both human queries and agent-driven loops.

P - primitive. A built-in compiler operation trusted by construction. Example: identifying the rising or falling state in an oscillation, or calculating how much a physical quantity has exceeded a threshold over time.

D - definition. A parameter or configuration chosen by the user or supplied from outside the compiler, such as window size.

O - object. The compiled output of a definition, such as the amplitudes, periods, or durations of individual waves in a sample.

M - measure. A derived quantitative value computed from one or more objects, such as average duration or maximum temporal asymmetry.

S - scientific interpretation. This is the layer outside the scope of the deterministic compiler. It is a claim about what the measures mean, written by a person or agent.

The current version of FeatureGraph is built specifically for oscillatory scientific and engineering signals, but the platform can be adapted and customized to work with other types of timeseries data. FeatureGraph does not retain or store raw data within the service, and only the constructed objects are available to be queried.

The current compiler is featuregraph-core, installable with pip install featuregraph-core. More on the architecture: compiler paper.

Using FeatureGraph with language models for data access

FeatureGraph is building out the option to use natural-language data retrieval. A demo on a small mockup table uses an agent built on Cohere’s Command A. The values in the table are not derived from real data. Cycle count here refers to the number of breaths in a recording, and mean symmetry is the mean per-breath symmetry for the recording.

A user question is sent as written:

Among confident CapnoBase cases, which are outliers in BOTH the number of detected cycles and mean temporal symmetry? An outlier is a value at least 1.5 sample standard deviations from the mean of that measure across the confident cases in that dataset.

The agent’s exposed response is a JSON query:

{
  "op": "intersect",
  "of": [
    {"op": "outliers", "measure": "cycle_count", "z": 1.5,
     "from": {"dataset": "capnobase", "is_confident": true}},
    {"op": "outliers", "measure": "mean_symmetry", "z": 1.5,
     "from": {"dataset": "capnobase", "is_confident": true}}
  ]
}

The agent itself writes the query, translating it from natural language, and a separate Python program outside the agent checks the query and runs it. It confirms that the query is well-formed, that the dataset it names exists in the table, and that it can run.

The query layer: ongoing development

The scientific interpretation or query layer in FeatureGraph is composed of 5 agent types.

Investigator: proposes hypotheses as labeled free text. Nothing becomes a finding until tested. It can be replaced by human-authored queries.

Tester: writes specs that run through an outside deterministic program called the executor, checked by validation and held-out data. This is the agent type built for the Command A demo linked above.

Critic: judges whether a stated finding follows from what was actually run.

Recorder: writes the provenance record from run logs.

Translator: maps a new domain’s vocabulary onto the schema. This role is deferred until a later release. For now, each domain’s choices are made by hand and recorded.

The developing stage is an agent loop that generates hypotheses and translates queries inside the language model, while the analysis itself runs outside it. This has two potential benefits:

  • The entire analysis can be tracked with receipts, rerun outside the loop, and checked for accuracy,
  • The loop can potentially be run on a more cost-efficient model than the frontier-size models that currently do open-ended research and hypothesis testing.

The output is a short, usually 2-3 page analysis stub that a human researcher can pick up, verify, and continue to build on. The existing research record can be found here.
entry.summary: Turning a time-series signal recording into a deterministic, reusable computational record.

entry.title: Learning World Models by Building One From Scratch

link.title: Learning World Models by Building One From Scratch

entry.content:
Intro:

Nahid Alam (https://www.linkedin.com/in/nahidalam/) is a researcher working on multimodal agents, with a focus on how reinforcement learning and world models can help agents understand, predict, and interact with their environments. Previously, she led Maya (github.com/nahidalam/maya), an open multilingual language model developed as a community research project within Cohere Labs.

What I am building

I am building World Models from Scratch, an open, hands-on project for understanding how video world models actually work by building one piece by piece. The goal is to go from an input video to a model that can predict possible future frames, while making every major step visible.

I want the project to be something people can run, modify, break, and learn from.

What is a World Model?

A world model learns how an environment changes over time and predicts what might happen next. It can help AI agents simulate possible futures and plan their actions.

Why I find it exciting

The idea of simulating different possible futures fascinates me, almost like the TV series Person of Interest. I often wonder how a different decision could have changed an outcome, or what life might have looked like if I had taken another path.

Technically, world models offer a way to simulate alternative futures and explore how different actions influence outcomes. This opens up exciting possibilities for counterfactual reasoning, planning, and decision-making in AI agents.

What Sparked it

World models are moving incredibly quickly. We are seeing models that can generate realistic video, simulate environments, support planning and decision-making. These systems feel like black boxes. It is easy to run them without really understanding what is happening inside.

I wanted to be in a different direction.

I wanted to see what happens at every stage. How does a video become something a Transformer can process? What does the model learn during training? How does it predict future frames? How can we make these models small enough for more people to experiment with them?

What I have actually done

We are building the book in the open, publishing as we go https://github.com/nahidalam/world_model_from_scratch

So far, we have run three sessions with the community. These sessions have been one of the most valuable parts of the project. People ask difficult questions, challenge assumptions, give active feedback, and build alongside the material.

The project is becoming a shared learning process rather than something I am building alone.

Why community matters

I hope this project becomes a useful learning resource for the community.

I want others to explore the code, train small models, test different ideas, and share what they discover. World models are developing quickly, and there are many open questions to explore.

Learning together can make these ideas easier to understand, more accessible to people who want to start experimenting with them and hopefully spark a new idea among them!

Where it is going

I hope the project becomes a go to resource for the community. As we learn more, I want to turn those lessons into code and explanations that make world models easier for others to build and understand.

Call to Action:

If you are curious about world models, come build with us.

Try the code and join one of our upcoming sessions https://luma.com/CLEmbodiedAI
entry.summary: Building video world models piece by piece through an open, hands-on community learning series.

entry.title: Tiny Aya Vision
entry.content:
Part of Expedition Tiny Aya. Code: Cohere-Labs-Community/expedition-tayavision. Results below reflect an in-progress v0 model, not a finished system.

What’s Tiny Aya Vision?

Tiny Aya Vision is an open-weight multilingual vision-language model (VLM) with fewer than 4B parameters, and it is the first of its kind. It extends Tiny Aya (3.35B, 70+ languages) with lightweight visual capabilities through parameter-efficient fusion strategies.

Core question: Can a small (~3B) multilingual language model gain effective visual grounding through parameter-efficient fusion without sacrificing multilingual text performance or on-device deployability?

Why This Matters

No existing sub-4B model combines vision capabilities with support for 70+ languages, particularly for low-resource languages.

Model Params Languages Vision
Tiny Aya Vision ~4B 70+ Yes
Qwen3-VL-2GB 2B ~32 Yes
Gemma 3-1B 1B 140+ Limited
SmolVLM <4B English-centric Yes
Ministral-3-3B 3.4B Basic multilingual Yes

Claim

Tiny Aya adds vision to a 3.35B multilingual (70+ languages) model using a frozen encoder, a small connector, and LoRA , then merges weights back to restore text performance. Aya Vision showed at 8B that this merging step does more than restore text performance. On AyaVisionBench, merging lifted multilingual vision win-rate against Pangea-7B from 58.1% to 70.0%, an 11.9 point gain over the unmerged checkpoint (Aya Vision, Fig. 12). The open question is whether the same gain appears at 3.35B, where there’s less parameter slack.

Evidence

Architecture

Tiny Aya Vision uses a late-fusion design, following Aya Vision and LLaVA : a frozen vision encoder produces patch embeddings, a trainable connector projects them into the language model’s embedding space, and the language model consumes them as ordinary input tokens.

Component Configurations Params Trained
Vision Encoder SigLIP2-so400m , 384x384 input ~400M Frozen
Connector Pixel Shuffle (2x2) + 2-layer SwiGLU MLP ~12M Stage 1
LLM backbone Tiny Aya Global, 70+ languages 3.35B Frozen
LLM adaptation LoRA, rank 256 ~280M Stage 2

An image enters SigLIP2 at 384×384 and comes out as 729 patch embeddings. Passing all of them to a 3.35B backbone is expensive relative to the model’s total budget, so Pixel Shuffle stacks each 2×2 neighbourhood along the embedding dimension, trading spatial resolution for depth and cutting the sequence to 196 tokens. The SwiGLU MLP then projects those into the backbone’s embedding space. Only the connector trains in Stage 1; LoRA is added in Stage 2 so the backbone can adapt to visual input without full fine-tuning.

Training Recipe

Training follows LLaVA’s two-stage recipe, previously validated by Aya Vision and Maya . In Stage 1 (alignment), we train only the connector on ~558K image–caption pairs (LLaVA-Pretrain), keeping both the vision encoder and the LLM frozen. This teaches the connector to map visual features into Tiny Aya’s embedding space. In Stage 2 (instruction tuning), we add LoRA (rank 256) to the LLM and move from English-only data (Milestone A) to a ~60/40 English/multilingual SFT mix (Milestone B), following the ratio Aya Vision found optimal at 8B.

We then add a training-free third step: cross-modal weight merging. The LLM weights are linearly interpolated between the fine-tuned multimodal checkpoint and the original text-only Tiny Aya Global,

W_merged = (1 − α) · W_text + α · W_mm

with the connector and vision encoder left unchanged. Aya Vision selected α = 0.4 at both 8B and 32B based on a sweep over interpolation weights (Fig. 9). At that setting, Aya Vision 8B limited text-only win-rate degradation on m-ArenaHard to 5.92% relative to the LLM it was initialized from, compared to 16.4% for Pangea-7B, 22.1% for Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and 44.1% for Molmo-7B (Fig. 5). Whether this behavior holds at 3.35B, where there is far less parameter redundancy to absorb the merge, remains an open question.

Benchmark Blind Score Notes
CVQA 25.60% Tiny Aya Global; chance ≈ 25% for 4-choice
Kaleidoscope 26.07% (avg) Range: 19% (Nepali) to 33.6% (Portuguese)
MaXM ~0.0% Generation task, impossible without images
MTVQA 0.0% Text reading in images, impossible without vision

Tiny Aya Global scores 25.6% on CVQA in the blind setting, with no image at all. After English-only alignment, it jumps to 45.5%, an increase of nearly 20 points, confirming real visual grounding rather than just language priors.

By language, Portuguese and Spanish lead (~50%+), reflecting the strength of high-resource, Latin-script languages. Sinhala is lowest (~21%), with Kinyarwanda and Oromo close behind (the lowest-resource languages), showing that this isn’t simply a script issue (Kinyarwanda and Oromo are Latin-script too). That gap is exactly what Milestone C’s culturally diverse visual data is designed to close.

Limitations

These results are early. The CVQA blind baseline sits at 25.6%, near chance, so it confirms the model gets real signal from images. But CVQA is partly language-solvable too. The gap is wide enough to show vision helps. It’s not wide enough to cleanly separate visual reasoning from language priors.

The per-language numbers here only cover Milestone A: English-only visual training. Milestone B (multilingual SFT) and Milestone C (culturally diverse visual data, a stretch goal) haven’t happened yet. Low-resource-language scores will likely look better once those land.

Cross-modal merging is also untested at this scale. At 8B, it recovered text performance and pushed vision win-rate up 20.5%. We don’t yet know if α=0.4 is still the right value at 3.35B, where the model has much less parameter redundancy to work with.

Two more open items: we haven’t run the MoonViT ablation, and we haven’t resolved the LoRA learning-rate discrepancy between Maya and Aya Vision at this scale.

Next Steps

A few things are still in progress. We’re running the merge ratio sweep (α = 0.3 to 0.7) at 3.35B to find whether the same Goldilocks zone from 8B holds here. We’re finishing Milestone B (multilingual SFT) and comparing it against Milestone A to isolate what explicit multilingual data adds on top of cross-lingual transfer. Milestone C, culturally diverse visual data from XM3600 , is a stretch goal we’ll pursue if time allows.

We also want to settle the LoRA learning-rate question left open by the Maya and Aya Vision comparison, and finish the MoonViT ablation to see if native-resolution encoding matters for script-heavy languages like Arabic or Thai.

Once results are final, we’ll release model weights on Hugging Face, publish the code, and report on-device latency numbers.
entry.summary: Extending Tiny Aya, a 3.35B multilingual model in 70+ languages, with lightweight visual capabilities through parameter-efficient fusion.

entry.title: Big Context Windows Are Not Memory: What I Learned When My Chats Kept Dying

link.title: Big Context Windows Are Not Memory: What I Learned When My Chats Kept Dying

entry.content:
The moment it broke

A few months back, I was working on a project and using ChatGPT for help and debugging. This was before I started using Claude Code. Things were going fine, and after a lot of back and forth, the model finally understood my project. It knew my file structure, my bugs, the fixes we had already tried. And right at that moment, the chat got full and forced me to start a new one.

That was the frustrating part. In the new chat, I had to explain everything again from zero. And even after explaining, the answers were not as accurate as the ones from the earlier session. All that built-up understanding was just gone.

Sitting there, I had one simple thought: why can’t it just compress or delete the older parts of the chat that are no longer useful? The recent stuff mattered. The stuff from an hour ago mostly didn’t. That one thought is what this whole post is about.

Going down the rabbit hole

As a student, I didn’t really know how these models worked inside. So I started digging. First videos, then articles, and eventually research papers.

Here is what I learned, in plain words. The model doesn’t read text the way we do. Your text gets broken into tokens, small chunks of words. The model can only “see” a fixed number of tokens at a time. That fixed size is called the context window. The model itself is an autoregressive transformer, which just means it writes one token at a time, always looking at everything currently inside the window to decide the next one.

The part that surprised me the most: the model has no memory at all. None. Every time you send a message, the entire chat history gets fed back into the window again. The model isn’t remembering your conversation. It is re-reading it, every single time. So when the window fills up, there is simply no room left for new messages. That is why my chat died.

Bigger window is not memory

The obvious fix, and the one every model release advertises, is a bigger window. 128K tokens. 200K. A million. If the window is huge, doesn’t the problem just go away?

Not really. When a model has more content sitting in its window, it has to spread its attention across all of it, including the parts that don’t matter anymore. That doesn’t just waste space. It actively makes the model worse at using the parts that do matter, even when the important information is technically still “in there.”

Here’s the part that changed how I thought about it. I found a paper from Google Research, Selective Attention Improves Transformer (ICLR 2025) . The first line of the abstract says it plainly: “Unneeded elements in the attention’s context degrade performance.” The authors show that cutting attention to unneeded tokens doesn’t just save memory, up to 47 times less memory for the attention part of the model. It also makes the model perform better, at the same quality.

That was a strange moment for me. My random frustration-thought, “just delete the stuff that’s no longer useful,” wasn’t just a convenience idea. Researchers had shown that removing stale context makes a model genuinely better, not just cheaper to run.

So the real problem was never window size. A context window is storage. Memory is something else: keeping what matters and dropping what doesn’t. A bigger window gives you more storage. It doesn’t give you that.

Context is a policy, not a feature

So I stopped reading about it and tried to build the policy myself. I called the project ContextShift, and it’s live here: context-shift.vercel.app.

The first version was small: a chat app with a hardcoded 4,000-token limit and two buttons, one to summarize the old messages, one to prune them. It worked. But the actual “decide what to keep” logic was just sitting inline in one file, wired to that one app. Nobody else could reuse it. Nobody could even ask, “what if we decided differently?”

So I pulled that decision out into its own idea. Not a feature bolted onto a chat app. A policy. And a policy, it turns out, is a surprisingly small thing to write down. Give it the messages so far and a token budget, and it hands back a decision: what to keep, what to drop.

class ContextStrategy(Protocol):
    def build(self, messages: Sequence[Message], budget: TokenBudget) -> ContextResult:
        ...

That’s the entire interface. One method. Nothing in it about summarizing, nothing about which model you’re using, nothing about buttons in a UI. Just: here’s what’s happened so far, here’s how much room you have, tell me what survives.

Once the decision had a shape like that, using it end to end became a few lines of code:

manager = ContextManager(
    strategy=PinnedRecencyStrategy(recent_buffer=2),
    provider=FakeLLMProvider(complete_response="Paris."),
    tokenizer=HeuristicTokenizer(),
    budget=TokenBudget(max_tokens=100, safety_margin=10),
)

result = manager.chat([], "What's the capital of France?")
print(result.response)  # "Paris."

Here’s how those pieces actually fit together:

The manager doesn’t know or care which policy it’s holding. That’s the whole point of writing the interface as one plain method instead of baking a specific strategy into the app. I could prove this to myself with something almost silly:

class DuckTypedStrategy:
    def build(self, messages, budget):
        return ContextResult(messages=list(messages), excluded=[])

isinstance(DuckTypedStrategy(), ContextStrategy)  # True

That class has never imported my library. It doesn’t inherit from anything. It just happens to have a method with the right name and shape, and that’s enough. “Pluggable” wasn’t a word I got to use because I said so. It’s a word I got to use because I could write a check like that one and watch it pass.

Once the shape was that small, writing a second policy, and then a third, and eventually a fourth, wasn’t a redesign. It was just writing the method again, differently. One keeps a fixed recency window and never drops anything you’ve pinned. One keeps as much of the recent conversation as fits the budget, with nothing fixed about it at all. One keeps a fixed number of the most recent messages, full stop, and treats the token budget as a backup limit instead of the main rule. And one doesn’t discard the older messages at all — it compresses them into a single summary and keeps that instead, the only policy that costs a real model call to decide.

Four different answers to the same question. Which raised the obvious next one: which answer is actually better?

Deciding what to keep, measured

Having four policies meant I could finally stop guessing which one was actually better. I could measure it. So I built a way to run every policy against the exact same conversation and compare what actually happens. Three of them fit this straight away, no model call involved anywhere — just the numbers: how many messages survive, how many tokens they cost, how long the decision takes. The fourth, the one that summarizes, needed a different kind of test, which I’ll get to.

from contextshift.benchmark import run_benchmark, to_markdown

results = run_benchmark(
    conversation,
    budget,
    [RecencyStrategy(), SlidingWindowStrategy(window_size=10), PinnedRecencyStrategy(recent_buffer=6)],
)
print(to_markdown(results))

On a 41-message conversation with a small budget, here’s what actually came out:

Strategy Kept Discarded Tokens Kept Tokens Discarded % Retained Latency (s)
RecencyStrategy 32 9 880 228 79.42% 0.000030
SlidingWindowStrategy 10 31 275 833 24.82% 0.000005
PinnedRecencyStrategy 33 8 888 220 80.14% 0.000028

That table is more honest than my gut ever was. The strategy that keeps a fixed number of messages leaves most of the budget on the table, 275 tokens used out of 900 available, because it cares about a predictable count, not a full window. The other two fill the budget almost completely. None of that is a guess anymore. It’s a number I can rerun any time I want.

That table told me how much of the budget each policy used. It didn’t tell me whether any of them kept the right things. A strategy that’s defined as “keep the last ten messages” reporting that it kept ten messages isn’t a finding — it’s the constructor argument, restated. I didn’t notice this for a while, because the numbers felt like evidence. They weren’t. They were just a description of how each policy is configured.

What actually tells you something is whether a policy drops the one message a later question depends on. So I built a second, harder benchmark: instead of counting messages, I hand-wrote a set of conversations where I knew, in advance, exactly which earlier message a later question needed — the name mentioned on turn one and asked about on turn forty, the correction that overwrote an earlier wrong answer, the pinned instruction sitting under a mountain of unrelated small talk. Then I ran every policy against all of them and checked whether that specific message survived.

The real number was worse than I expected. Across the fixture set, every policy loses more than half of what the questions actually depend on. The best of them, the one that pins important messages, keeps 40%. Not 90%. Forty. The two without pinning do worse — one keeps as little as 13% of what actually mattered, even while it was filling most of its token budget with something. That’s the distinction the first table couldn’t show: two policies can retain a near-identical share of tokens while one of them is quietly throwing away the parts of the conversation that made the model useful in the first place.

While I was building the third policy, something happened that I didn’t expect. I’d written a plain, budget-driven strategy: no fixed window, no pinning, just keep as much of the recent conversation as fits. I assumed it would behave differently from the other two. So I wrote a test comparing it against the pinned-and-windowed strategy, using a window of exactly one message.

The test told me they were identical. Not similar. Identical, message for message, for every conversation with no pinned messages in it.

I had spent real time building a “new” policy that turned out to be a special case of one I already had. My first reaction was mild embarrassment. My second reaction was that this is actually a good sign. It meant the interface was small enough that a genuinely new idea and an old idea wearing a different name would show up as the same thing under a fair test. If I hadn’t measured it, I would never have known. I would have just believed I’d built three different things.

Full circle

That gave me real confidence in the idea itself. And not long after, I found out I wasn’t the only one who’d landed on it.

Some time later, I started using Claude Code for my own projects. And there it was: a built-in compact feature that summarizes the older parts of a session when it gets full. The exact thing I’d been missing during that ChatGPT session, and the thing I’d tried to build myself, was already shipping in a production tool.

That felt like real confirmation. The tools people actually rely on didn’t solve this by waiting for a bigger window. They solved it by managing context on top of the window: summarizing what’s old, dropping what’s stale. Long-term memory for LLMs isn’t something you get for free from a bigger number. It’s something you build on top of the window, not inside it.

What I’d tell other

This whole thing started from an annoyance, not a course or an assignment. Chasing one small “why is this so annoying?” question taught me more about tokenization, attention, and interface design than any tutorial I had watched before.

I want to be honest about where the edges still are. More than once while building this, I felt the pull to add a way to pick a policy by name from a list, some kind of menu. Each time, the honest answer was the same: there was nothing to choose between yet. A menu with one real option isn’t a menu. Saying no to that turned out to matter more than most of the things I said yes to.

The bigger honest edge used to be this: I could measure how many tokens a policy keeps, and how fast it decides, but not whether the answers you get afterward are actually better. That gap is smaller now — there’s an opt-in mode that asks a real model each question and scores the actual answer, not just whether the right message survived. But I built that carefully, separate from everything else, because it costs money and isn’t deterministic the moment you turn it on, and I haven’t yet pointed it at a conversation of my own and watched what comes back. The honest edge just moved: I know the plumbing works. I don’t yet know what it says.

The library is open source on GitHub, and you can also try the live demo. Try it, break it, tell me what fails. That’s still the part of open science I like the most: you don’t need permission to start pulling on a thread.
